text: The center of mass is where the rocket balances. The center of pressure is where the air pushes. Keep the balance point ahead of the push point. Then the nose stays forward. Fins pull the push point back. Aim for one to two body widths of gap.

text: The stability margin, in calibers, is the center of gravity minus the raw center of pressure, divided by the reference diameter. Stations are measured in meters from the base, positive up. A positive margin means the balance point is ahead of the push point, so the stack is stable on the pad. The hangar marker clamps the drawn center of pressure to the nose, but the margin keeps the raw value. The estimate uses full tanks at liftoff, landing reserve included. It is not the max-Q case, when much of the propellant is already gone. Finned or unguided rockets aim for one to two calibers. Above four calibers, the designer warns that the rocket is overstable and will weathercock. An unguided rocket with a negative margin is blocked. A steered stage without fins gets a note instead, because the engines can point the stack. Grid fins add mass and drag. They do not move the center of pressure.

text: An orbit is a fall that keeps missing Earth. A two hundred kilometer circle moves at about seven point eight kilometers per second. A four hundred kilometer circle is slower, about seven point seven kilometers per second. Pier 7 already moves at about zero point four one kilometers per second. That ground speed is free.

text: Closed-orbit speed at periapsis is the square root of mu, times two over the periapsis radius, minus two over the sum of periapsis and apoapsis radii. Each radius is Earth's radius plus that altitude. Mu is Earth's gravitational parameter, three point nine eight six zero zero four four one eight times ten to the fourteenth cubic meters per second squared, and Earth's radius is six million three hundred seventy-eight thousand one hundred thirty-seven meters. A two hundred kilometer circle is about seven thousand seven hundred eighty-four meters per second. Four hundred kilometers is about seven thousand six hundred sixty-nine. The five hundred fifty kilometer sun-synchronous target is about seven thousand five hundred eighty-five. A geostationary transfer orbit, two hundred by thirty-five thousand seven hundred eighty-six kilometers, is about ten thousand two hundred thirty-nine at periapsis. Required delta-v then subtracts site rotation at twenty-eight point five degrees latitude, about four hundred nine meters per second, and adds fifteen hundred meters per second of losses. That is about eight thousand eight hundred seventy-six for two hundred kilometers, eight thousand seven hundred sixty for four hundred, eight thousand six hundred seventy-six for the sun-synchronous target, and eleven thousand three hundred thirty for the transfer orbit. Inclination does not change this budget. Latitude does. The suborbital one hundred kilometer target is not a closed orbit. Its budget is about two thousand four hundred meters per second.

text: The booster keeps some propellant for the trip home. That reserve does not count toward orbit. On Haven, a soft centered touchdown is Perfect. A tip, or a miss of the deck, is Salvage. A water landing is not graded.

tags: neutral: Codex read-aloud; separate codex audio manifest; text = data/codex.json, spoken form
text: The landing reserve is a set mass of propellant. The designer allows zero to thirty percent of that stage's propellant. The game will not count more reserve than the propellant loaded. Only the rest enters the rocket equation. The reserve rides as dry mass, so the stack still lifts it. Legs multiply the first stage's dry mass by one point zero six. Grid fins add one hundred twenty kilograms per square meter of the stage's cross section. Steering jets add two hundred fifty kilograms. The ascent sim does not fly the landing burn. Haven's grade compares two margins. Sink margin is one, minus the absolute sink rate over the allowed landing speed. Offset margin is one, minus the absolute miss distance over the allowed tolerance. The grade uses the smaller one. Water is ungraded. On a deck, a tip, or either margin below zero, is Salvage. Zero point four five or better is Perfect. Zero point two or better is Good. Anything else on the deck is Hard.
